implementation_notes: java.util.PriorityQueue is the library's binary heap - a MIN-heap by default, with offer, poll, peek, and a bulk constructor that heapifies in O(n). It is not thread-safe: for concurrent use, java.util.concurrent.PriorityBlockingQueue wraps it with a lock, which is the right answer for a scheduler and the wrong one under high contention. A monotonic sequence counter is the standard tie-breaker (priority, seq, task) so equal priorities are FIFO and the comparator never falls through to comparing tasks. PriorityQueue does not support decrease-key; for Dijkstra with a real frontier, either use an indexed heap with a position map or use lazy deletion with a distance check on pop.
idiom_name: java.util.PriorityQueue (min-heap) or PriorityBlockingQueue for concurrent use; a monotonic sequence for tie-breaking
pitfalls: PriorityQueue is not thread-safe - concurrent offer/poll needs PriorityBlockingQueue, which introduces a lock and its contention.
No decrease-key; for Dijkstra with a real frontier, use an indexed heap or lazy deletion (re-push and skip stale entries on pop).
Comparator.comparingInt(priority) alone ties on equal priorities and then throws or misbehaves; add thenComparing on a monotonic sequence.
iterator() does not return elements in priority order; to drain in order, poll repeatedly.
